projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Harry Shiveley was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Mason
sp.p: And that should be recording I checked it before. That works pretty well. The Library of Congress would like us to get some basic information on there so they can listen to it and

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: Right

sp.speaker: Thomas Mason
sp.p: They'd like your name, your birthdate, and your current address.

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: Ok, it's Harry Shiveley, S-h-i-v-e-1-e-y. Current address is 910 Westwood Drive, Vienna, Virginia, and what do you need? My age?

sp.speaker: Thomas Mason
sp.p: Ah, I guess your birthdate is one thing they ask for.

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: Oh, 15 August, 1919

sp.speaker: Thomas Mason
sp.p: Ok, and the interviewers are Thomas Mason and...

sp.speaker: Will Cromartie
sp.p: Will Cromartie

sp.speaker: Thomas Mason
sp.p: And my affiliation with the interviewee is I'm his neighbor. And that should cover just sort of the basics that they want to know.

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: Alright

sp.speaker: Thomas Mason
sp.p: We were wondering, well, to start off, what wars you were in?

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: We made the invasion in Normandy, in World War 2, then from there I went to Kor, to Korea, fought all the way through that.

sp.speaker: Will Cromartie
sp.p: Um, were you drafted or did you enlist?

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: No I was already in the service.

sp.speaker: Will Cromartie
sp.p: How long had you been in the service?

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: I, I stayed in about twenty years.

sp.speaker: Thomas Mason
sp.p: Wow .

sp.speaker: Will Cromartie
sp.p: Previous, how long had you been in before World War One broke out?

sp.speaker: Thomas Mason
sp.p: World War Two.

sp.speaker: Will Cromartie
sp.p: World War Two, yeah.

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: Uh, I had been in the service about three months.

sp.speaker: Thomas Mason
sp.p: We were wondering what, what had made you want to join the service? (Pause)

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: Well in, that time there went many jobs anywhere, so I wanted to keep it busy. So I joined the national guard, which only meant once a week (pause) and (clears throat) we went to camp in summer. And when the World War Two broke out and they federalized the national guard (pause, clears throat) So I became active duty. (Pause) What else?

sp.speaker: Thomas Mason
sp.p: We uh, were wondering, well, what branch of the service you served in was

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: Field artillery

sp.speaker: Thomas Mason
sp.p: For the Army?

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: For the Army.

sp.speaker: Thomas Mason
sp.p: They, well, they wanted to know what your highest rank was.

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: Lieutenant-Colonel.

sp.speaker: Thomas Mason
sp.p: And they were also wondering, uh, you mentioned where you served, we were wondering after World War Two what prompted you to remain in the Army throughout Korea as well?

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: I liked it. And, and jobs were hard to find at that time, so I just stayed in.

sp.speaker: Will Cromartie
sp.p: What was your opinions of the Generals Eisenhower and MacArthur?

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: I never served under MacArthur. I respected both two generals very much.

sp.speaker: Thomas Mason
sp.p: We were wondering, uh, Could you recall your first days in training or in the service or, as you said, the national guard?

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: Well, in the national guard it was once a week, like it is now. And every summer we'd go to camp for two months. And it was, I enjoyed it very much. I also had a job working. In, in national guard at that time was one day a week. And then in summer we'd go out to camp for three months, one month.

sp.speaker: Thomas Mason
sp.p: We were, uh, wondering if you could tell us what your experiences were like during training before you were shipped out?

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: Well, by that time I was used to it pretty well. We went to camp, every summer. I enjoyed it. Then we met once a week for national guard duty.

sp.speaker: Will Cromartie
sp.p: Do you remember your instructors?

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: They were regular Army Seargents. I don't remember their names.

sp.speaker: Thomas Mason
sp.p: Do you remember what they were like? Just sort of, you know, their personalities or anything like that?

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: Yes I enjoyed them very much. And they respected us. So we had a good, relationship.

sp.speaker: Thomas Mason
sp.p: Oh um, you mentioned you were in the national guard and that you were fairly used to training. Well, we remember some people had hard times getting through boot camp. We were wondering how you got, or how was your time getting through it?

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: No problems. (Clears throat) At that time jobs were hard to find. So if you had a good assignment we held on to it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Mason
sp.p: We were ah, wondering, did you make any, friends while you were at boot camp that you stayed close to throughout your term of service?

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: No, I've not, I don't remember any of the, I don't have any good friends from earlier training.

sp.speaker: Will Cromartie
sp.p: What was your first assignment after boot camp?

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: Well the, (Clears throat) well this, this was in the Kentucky National Guard, and there weren't too many well educated troops there. I had a high school education. I could read and write, and, I became the battery clerk, which does all the paperwork. They were glad to have me because I could read. (Pause)

sp.speaker: Thomas Mason
sp.p: We ah, we wanted to know, ah, when you went over to World War Two, some people liked to bring good luck charms with them when they went. We were wondering if you brought anything to remember home with you?

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: No I, the only thing I wanted to have with me was a pistol and a rifle, which I had. I had no good luck charm.

sp.speaker: Will Cromartie
sp.p: Did you keep in contact with anyone back home?

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: Certainly, with my family. I wasn't married then. So my mother, and sister. We kept in touch, by letters.

sp.speaker: Thomas Mason
sp.p: I believe you answered our next question as well with that one. I ah, (pause) when you were in your unit I was wondering what you thought of the other people you served with?

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: Well I liked them. We (clears throat) We had to work together, and once we went into, into battle, then you depended on them and they depended on you. So we got along very well.

sp.speaker: Thomas Mason
sp.p: Do you remember any of them clearly or especially like the was there a unit prankster or joker or anything that stood out?

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: (clears throat) I don't rememb, I don't remember any, thing like that. By the time, by the time we got into war you depended on everybody else around you and, by the same token they depended on you. (Pause)

sp.speaker: Thomas Mason
sp.p: Um, can you recall any particular friends from when you served?

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: No, In my national guard days there was a first Sargent, I remember him. He was very good. But then, I left there to go into officers candidate school. So I, I lost touch with all of them. I became part of the regular army, at that time.

sp.speaker: Thomas Mason
sp.p: We ah, we remember that when we were looking up about the wars that some people had mixed feelings about the people they were fighting. We were wondering what your opinions of the ah, well the enemy during the war was?

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: Well they were enemy, (laughs), and they were kill or be killed. And that's the way we fought the war, (pause) until we got into occupation. And then, they became our friends.

sp.speaker: Will Cromartie
sp.p: Serving in Europe what did you know about what was happening in uh, the, Pacific.

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: We had, radio, we had, the daily briefings. So we were pretty well up to date on everything.

sp.speaker: Thomas Mason
sp.p: We ah, we also wanted to know, I remember at one point you mentioned you were a aerial observer for the Army's artillery.

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: Yes, first I was a observer. Then I became an Army pilot, flew my own airplanes. I had an observer in the back seat. So that was a daily job in the war. Went off early in the morning, look for targets, and then fly all day and come back. Cause these were small planes we'd have to come back and (clears throat) land and refuel. Then go back and

sp.speaker: Will Cromartie
sp.p: What type of plane was it?

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: An L-4 piper cub. Sixty five horsepower, which is very small.

sp.speaker: Thomas Mason
sp.p: We were wondering ah, overall what the job was like. Was it rather stressful or one of those where you have sort of long periods of silence?

sp.speaker: Will Cromartie
sp.p: Was it tedious?

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: No, not France, especially up in Normandy, it was very exciting you get shot at every day. And you try to direct your artillery at who was shooting at you. So that you could silence them. I apologize for this voice, sorry.

sp.speaker: Thomas Mason
sp.p: It's no problem. (Pause) That sounds like an inherently dangerous job, but it was exciting for you at times?

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: Yeh (clears throat) yeh it was dangerous and it was exciting at the same time. Especially when you got shot at. But these L-4's were made of canvas. So frequently you would come back with holes in the airplane. But I was never shot down.

sp.speaker: Will Cromartie
sp.p: Were you afraid of being shot down?

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: There was always that possibility, sure.

sp.speaker: Will Cromartie
sp.p: Did you try to block that out though?

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: Yeh, but we were always in communication with our own troops. So if we were getting shot at we would tell them where they, who was shooting at us, where from, and direct artillery fire on them. So it became exciting that way.

sp.speaker: Thomas Mason
sp.p: It ah, it almost seems that they would be hesitant to shoot at you if you were an artillery observer. You'd think that would give away their position.

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: Well, they became very cagy about that. You got to fly and turn around every now and then and, and as soon as you'd turn around they'd shoot, thinking you couldn't see them. But, we'd go out with two aircraft so that one of them could always watch. And whenever they shot at you we would radio where they were. And immediately our, our artillery would blast them. Shut, shut 'em up in a hurry.

sp.speaker: Thomas Mason
sp.p: Ah, our next question was, hugh, did you ever see combat but, considering you got shot at every moment-

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: (laughs)

sp.speaker: Thomas Mason
sp.p: It answers itself.

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: Yes always every time we went up we'd get shot at. So sure, I saw combat all the time.

sp.speaker: Thomas Mason
sp.p: Did you ever wish that you could shoot back?

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: Well, the only thing I had on me was a 45 pistol on my hip, and couldn't do much with that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Mason
sp.p: I suppose not.

sp.speaker: Will Cromartie
sp.p: You said you were never shot down but you also said you'd come back and see big holes in the canvas. Were there any particular close calls where you come back and realize, could have been dangerous?

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: Yes there were several. (Clears throat) And ah, and ah, knew I was hit. You could hear the bullets go through the canvas. And I'd ah, hightail it out of there.

sp.speaker: Will Cromartie
sp.p: Did that make it particularly, particularly hard to fly?

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: No, you mean?

sp.speaker: Will Cromartie
sp.p: Shot up.

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: You mean the aircraft or me?

sp.speaker: Will Cromartie
sp.p: Ah, with the aircraft being shot up.

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: Uh, unless they hit the engine, you'd just have canvas all around you and you could fly back. And it wouldn't hurt, wouldn't hurt to fly at all.

sp.speaker: Thomas Mason
sp.p: Did it make you nervous when the planes got, started to get shot at?

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: Well it wasn't, (laughs), it wasn't very fun, no. (cough) But if anything it made me mad. So you had to back off, try to remember where they were shooting from. And, and I had a lot of heavy artillery behind me. I could call it in on them. Shut 'em up in a hurry.

sp.speaker: Thomas Mason
sp.p: Um, when they were shooting bullets at your aircraft were you ever wounded during your tour of duty?

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: No, never was. Ah, we tried not to get too low, to have them be able to shoot at us with rifles, or machine guns. Unless they hit the engine they wouldn't hurt us, shoot holes in the aircraft. No problems.

sp.speaker: Will Cromartie
sp.p: How'd you deal with the stress? Flying all these missions, being shot at all the time?

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: (laughs) You come back and they'd have a, a shot of whisky waiting for you, which I took. After we got down on the ground, and everybody laughed about it, made it through another one.

sp.speaker: Will Cromartie
sp.p: What does it feel like coming back from a mission getting back on the ground?

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: Wonderful, real good.

sp.speaker: Will Cromartie
sp.p: How long did you have between missions and what did you do in that time?

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: Well, (clears throat) sometimes I'd go up four times a day. And you'd come back, look at the maps, talk to your headquarters by radio. And they would tell you to examine certain areas, which we did.

sp.speaker: Thomas Mason
sp.p: I guess we don't have to ask you if you were a prisoner of war if you were never shot down.

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: I wasn't shot down as such. But when my plane got down on the ground the mechanics shook their heads. (Laughs) Caused them a lot of work to get it back in shape again.

sp.speaker: Thomas Mason
sp.p: Were there any ah, were there any memorable experiences when you got back on the ground?

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: No, not other than you're glad to be back all in one piece. No big problems at all.

sp.speaker: Thomas Mason
sp.p: I was more thinking, you were mentioning the mechanics how they were irritated that your plane would come back looking like Swiss cheese.

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: Yeh they hated it. (Laughs) But in a way they were glad that the airplane was back because you develop a certain love for your airplane, and the mechanics hated to see it shot up.

sp.speaker: Will Cromartie
sp.p: Did you name your plane?

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: Yes, I was from Kentucky at the time, so she was Kentucky ba, Kentucky Babe.

sp.speaker: Thomas Mason
sp.p: Was there any particular experience that stands out in your mind in your time in the service?

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: In the service or during the war?

sp.speaker: Thomas Mason
sp.p: Um, in either.

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: No, , after the war I came home, and, and married. Incidently my wife is a first Lieutenant in the Army. She's a nurse.

sp.speaker: Will Cromartie
sp.p: Did you marry between the wars or after Korea?

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: After, no, in between World War Two and Korea.

sp.speaker: Will Cromartie
sp.p: What else did you do in between the wars?

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: I had a job, and uh, I went back to the national guard, once a week drill. Every summer with maneuvers.

sp.speaker: Thomas Mason
sp.p: Did you stay on as an aerial observer during Korea?

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: Sure did. But I was a pilot, and I had some poor soul in the back seat who was supposed to be directing the artillery. It wa, Korea was I think worse that World War Two, because you never knew for sure where the Koreans were.

sp.speaker: Will Cromartie
sp.p: How were your assignments different in Korea?

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: It, It was more frequent. It was, we would fly more often because the Koreans were very adept at creeping forward, and shooting at us at all times.

sp.speaker: Thomas Mason
sp.p: You mentioned that the ah, observer behind you was a poor soul. Is there any particular reason why?

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: (Laughs) Well I had control of the airplane and I'm sure he would liked to have control and turn around and gone back. But, I was bound and determined to get him up where the action was. However we developed a very good relationship between the pilot and the observer.

sp.speaker: Will Cromartie
sp.p: Did you keep the same observer?

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: In, In most cases we did but we'd have to rotate around. They'd send a new observer along to get some experience. But you, you would like to always keep the same guy once you got used to him. We were really good that way. As a matter of fact the observers would come live out at the airstrip with us. So that when we'd take off early in the morning and we, we were all there together.

sp.speaker: Thomas Mason
sp.p: Do you remember any of them? In particular, the observers? &

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: I don't remember their names. No, because we had so many.

sp.speaker: Will Cromartie
sp.p: Urn, were you, had you been able to stay in touch with any of them or anyone else from your service?

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: No, I haven't kept in touch with any of them.

sp.speaker: Thomas Mason
sp.p: You mentioned you lived out at the airstrip, what was that like in terms of, ah living conditions?

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: Well it, (Laughs), for one thing you very rarely ever took your clothes off. You just lay down in the sack, the sleeping bag, got whatever sleep you could get. Then you'd take your shoes off. Then, every now and again you'd get to go back, for rest and recuperation, R and R we'd call it. In which case you could get to go back somewhere. But while we were up, up on duty we'd sleep in our clothes, take shoes off. And had a twenty-four hour alert. Somebody's awake at all times.

sp.speaker: Will Cromartie
sp.p: How was the food?

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: (Laughs) It was GI. It was the GI rations and they, they were good. When we got to France we'd swap our GI food for some of their French food. They were glad to get our food because it was so good. I mean, so nutritious, didn't necessarily taste good all the time. But it was good it was meat, and there's no meat or anything in, eh France.

sp.speaker: Will Cromartie
sp.p: How did the living conditions compare between the wars?

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: You mean between?

sp.speaker: Will Cromartie
sp.p: How did the living conditions in Korea compare to the living conditions during World War Two?

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: Oh, well the living conditions were, you'd be in a tent somewhere and ah, it's the same no matter where you go.

sp.speaker: Thomas Mason
sp.p: No problems with more mosquitoes in Korea or something like that?

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: No, if you didn't take your clothes off, you put a net over your head that, that's all you needed. No problems.

sp.speaker: Will Cromartie
sp.p: What did ah the soldiers do for entertainment?

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: Well there weren't any women around, (Laughs), so we'd just shoot at the enemy. When we got a chance--fortey five--we were playing cards all the time. Poker, bridge, or breaking in a new observer.

sp.speaker: Thomas Mason
sp.p: What do you mean?

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: Getting him used to it. If you could fly you'd take him out, and make sure he could read the map, and tell you what you'd seen. So you'd be flying the plane up in the front but he's in the back seat. He doesn't see as well as you do. You have to tell him where you're going, and he's trying to trace you on the map. And frequently the observer had to tell you how to get back to where you came from, cause you're too busy flying the aircraft. And looking and steer.

sp.speaker: Thomas Mason
sp.p: It's almost as though you were the observer up in front being able to see better.

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: Well that's right. But ah, the observer had the radio earphones, although I had earphones too but, he did all the communicating, and kept pinpointing where we were. And when you'd talk to the base camp, they'd tell us to look at a certain point and he pick it out on the map and tell me where to go to find it.

sp.speaker: Will Cromartie
sp.p: Which did you like being better, did you like being the observer or the pilot?

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: The Pilot.

sp.speaker: Will Cromartie
sp.p: The pilot, because you have control?

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: Sure, (laughs) you could always dive down in a hurry to get out of it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Mason
sp.p: You mentioned you went to war with a rifle. What did you do before you were a pilot in the Army?

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: I was an usher in a theatre, movie theatre. And then, and that's it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Mason
sp.p: What jobs did you do in the Army before you were a pilot?

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: I was the battery clerk. See this was the Kentucky National guard and not everybody was educated at all, could read or write. But because I could read and write, and type, I became a very important part of, of the staff.

sp.speaker: Will Cromartie
sp.p: Is that why you went to officers school?

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: Yes, they, they decided they needed me. Anybody who could read and write was a likely candidate to go to OCS, officer candidate school.

sp.speaker: Thomas Mason
sp.p: Did you go straight from being a battery clerk to a pilot?

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: No, I went to, I went from a battery clerk into officer candidate school, and became a second Lieutenant. And, not until after that did I go to pilot school.

sp.speaker: Thomas Mason
sp.p: What was pilot school like?

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: Oh, a, some big guy sitting in the back seat hollering at ya.

sp.speaker: Will Cromartie
sp.p: When did you first get to Europe?

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: 1943 sometime.

sp.speaker: Thomas Mason
sp.p: You mentioned you were at the offensive on Normandy. Were you there during or after D- Day?

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: Well D-Day was the the infantry had to go and find us a place to land. So all during D-Day I sat on the landing ship and the landing craft, it wasn't a big boat. But my airplane was, had its wings taken off, tied to the sides. But as soon as the infantry got a few, cow pastures for us to land in we'd, your boat would take your stuff to the beach, put the airplanes off on the beach, take 'em to the first grassy field you could find, put the wings back on, and take off, look for targets.

sp.speaker: Thomas Mason
sp.p: Um, did you as an observer, did a lot of the people in you squadron, I don't know if you'd fly in a squadron as an observer, but, did many of your copilots and observers, were many of them wounded in the war?

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: Uh, one of the pilots was shot up pretty well. But he managed to bring the aircraft back, so we patched up the airplane sent him off to the hospital. Got a new pilot, it was a routine thing. No problem.

sp.speaker: Thomas Mason
sp.p: Um, were you awarded any medals or citations during your service?

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: Well I got the air medal, I got the occupation medal, and I got the, all the medals that they gave all the troops for being in the war. I don't remember them. But um, I wasn't wounded, so I didn't get a purple heart. No, I guess I did get a purple heart but, because I, I made a crash on the aircraft. So, I hurt my arm a little. But a, I wasn't shot anywhere at all.

sp.speaker: Thomas Mason
sp.p: You mentioned you crashed. What was, what was the experience of being in that aircraft as it went down?

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: Well the first thing you do as you're going down is you're looking for a place to land. Get the aircraft in, in a place where you can at least see. The observer in the meantime is talking on the radio to our other planes to let them know where we are. As soon as you get down on the ground you bail out of the aircraft, and wait for some, for the infantry to come. Then they'd fly in some infantry in on, on a field to take you out.

sp.speaker: Will Cromartie
sp.p: Did you and your observer come out of this relatively unhurt?

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: Yes, you could land those little L-4's anywhere. on

sp.speaker: Will Cromartie
sp.p: So this was during World War One?

sp.speaker: Will Cromartie
sp.p: Two, second time, so this was during World War Two?

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: Do I really look that old?

sp.speaker: Will Cromartie
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Mason
sp.p: We have problems with numbers.

sp.speaker: Will Cromartie
sp.p: So this was during World War Two though?

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: World War Two yes.

sp.speaker: Will Cromartie
sp.p: What did you fly in Korea?

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: Well we got L-4's and L-5's, a bigger airplane.

sp.speaker: Will Cromartie
sp.p: Oh, moving up.

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: Moving up a little.

sp.speaker: Thomas Mason
sp.p: Were there any memorable stories that stick out in your mind from your times um in the Army?

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: I don't think so.

sp.speaker: Will Cromartie
sp.p: Did you keep a diary or journal?

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: No, we, we were told not to because if we ever got shot down and you had it with you that would give aid to the enemy.

sp.speaker: Will Cromartie
sp.p: Do you have the letters, have some sort of records?

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: Well a, those that I mailed home. I wasn't married then, I mailed them to my mother.

sp.speaker: Thomas Mason
sp.p: Were you ever afraid that ah, and you mentioned that they fired from ground upon your aircraft. Were you ever afraid that German aircraft might come and try to chase you down?

sp.speaker: Harry Shiveley
sp.p: We had several of them try. But all you had to do was.."pull a sharp dive and loose them. They couldn't turn all that well."
